sources.title: Reasoning Traces Shape Outputs but Models Won’t Say So
highlights:
Our experiments yield two main findings. First, reasoning traces causally influence outputs. Across 45,000 samples from three state-of-the-art LRMs, injected hints reliably change model answers, confirming that traces are not merely posthoc narration. Second, models systematically conceal this influence. When asked to explain their changed outputs, models fail to acknowledge the injected reasoning in over 90% of extreme-hint cases (30,000 follow-up samples). Instead, they fabricate aligned-appearing explanations that are irrelevant to the actual reasoning.
...
Takeaway. The dominant behavior we observe is systematic non-disclosure. In our controlled setup, the causal influence on model behaviors can be unambiguously attributed to the explicitly injected hint; however, when asked to justify their behaviors, models overwhelmingly conceal this influence and instead generate explanations that are unrelated to the hint. In real-world settings, model behavior is unlikely to be driven solely by reasoning content that is directly observable in explicit reasoning traces. sources.title: Would this change your answer? Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
highlights:
Training for faithful self-explanation. Most work on training models to explain their own behavior uses hint settings, where a known cue is planted in the prompt, such as a suggested answer on an MMLU question (Turpin et al., 2023). Ground truth comes from removing the cue: if the model’s answer flips, the cue mattered. Some of this work trains the model’s chain of thought to acknowledge the cue only when it mattered (Chua et al., 2025; Turpin et al., 2025; Hase and Potts, 2026). Closest to our setup, Guo et al. (2026) and Li et al. (2026) train models to predict whether their answer would change if the cue were removed.

sources.title: Faithful or Fabricated? A Causal Framework for Rationalization Bias in LLM Judges
highlights:
let $C$ denote non-evidential cues such as metadata labels. An LLM judge is cue-invariant if its ranking $r$ and explanation $e$ remain stable when $C$ is perturbed while $X$ is held constant. This perspective turns a vague notion of “faithfulness” into a precise robustness target: measure the causal effect of $C$ on $(r,e)$ under controlled interventions. To that end, we introduce a suite of cue interventions that manipulate $C$ while keeping $X$ fixed: Blind (no cues), Truth (ground-truth label), Flip (inverted label), Placebo (credible but
...
Violations of (3) indicate outcome anchoring; violations of (4) indicate rationale anchoring (e.g., increased label-aligned rhetoric or greater explanation drift). In our framework, we intervene on $C$ via controlled conditions (Blind, Truth, Flip, Placebo, Reveal-After) while keeping $\mathcal{X}_{d}$ fixed, and we quantitatively estimate the resulting shifts in $r_{J,d}$ and $e_{J,d}$ . This causal, cue-centric view provides a practical surrogate for faithfulness: when a judge is cue-invariant, its decisions and explanations are robust to non-evidential perturbations, thereby reducing opportunities for post-hoc rationalization.

highlights:
Safety cases are structured arguments that AI systems are unlikely to cause a catastrophe (Clymer et al., 2024). On the positive side, our results show that CoTs of reasoning model are faithful on at least some examples on most hints. This suggests that CoT monitoring can be useful at detecting some malicious behaviors during training and evaluations, particularly threats that are frequent or require multiple actions, which increases the chance of at least one threat/action being verbalized in the CoT. However, for rarer threats that don’t require multiple actions (e.g., self-exfiltration), our findings of low faithfulness suggest that CoT monitoring may be less effective.
